stem:
Every July, as part of a research project, Rita collects data about sightings of a particular kind of bird. Each day in July she notes whether she sees this kind of bird or not, and she records the number $X$ of days on which she sees it. She models the distribution of $X$ by $\text{B}(31, p)$, where $p$ is the probability of seeing this kind of bird on a randomly chosen day in July.

Data from previous years suggests that $p = 0.3$, but in 2022 Rita suspected that the value of $p$ had been reduced. She decided to carry out a hypothesis test.

In July 2022, she saw this kind of bird on 4 days.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Use the binomial distribution to test at the 5% significance level whether Rita’s suspicion is justified.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: In July 2023, she noted the value of $X$ and carried out another test at the 5% significance level using the same hypotheses.
parts.text: Calculate the probability of a Type I error.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Rita models the number of sightings, $Y$, per year of a different, very rare, kind of bird by the distribution $\text{B}(365, 0.01)$.

parts.label: (i)
parts.text: Use a suitable approximating distribution to find $\text{P}(Y = 4)$.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.text: Justify your approximating distribution in this context.
